newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC adopts overhaul of phone charges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC adopts overhaul of phone charges.

text.p: Regulators Wednesday adopted an historic overhaul of the nation's complex web of telephone charges aimed at fostering fiercer competition and lower prices in the $200 billion per year phone industry.

The new rules, approved at a public meeting, stem from last year's communications law. Federal Communications Commission officials predicted the overhall will deliver $25 billion in lower phone costs to residential and business phone customers over the next five years.
"This is the single best day that business and residential customers have had since the (1984) breakup of AT&T," FCC Chairman Reed Hundt said.
Basic residential phone rates are intended to stay at current levels.
Businesses and residences who make lots of long-distance calls will see their monthly phone bill drop the most.
But residential and business customers with more than one phone line and who make few or no long-distance calls are expected to see their costs rise.
-- Reduce in July by $1.7 billion the $23 billion in annual charges long-distance carriers pay local companies to access their networks.
-- Reduce access charges by a total of $18.5 billion over the next five years.
-- Lower the permanent access charge of 5.4 cents a minute by one cent a minute in 1998 and reduce it over time to one cent on either end of a call.
-- Keep the monthly "subscriber line charge" customers pay to the local phone company at $3.50.
-- Boost the charge for residential customers with more than one line to $5 a month from $3.50, and to roughly $7 from $6 for multi-line businesses.
